---
title: "Latent-factor generalized linear models"
description: "Interactive effects with covariates, masks, offsets, and non-Gaussian responses."
---

## Interactive rather than additive heterogeneity

An additive unit effect shifts every period equally. Interactive effects allow
units to respond differently to common shocks:

$$
\eta_{it}=X_{it}'\beta+A_i'B_t+o_{it},\qquad
E[Y_{it}\mid X,A,B]=g^{-1}(\eta_{it}).
$$

`LatentFactorGLM` supports Gaussian/identity, Bernoulli/logit and Poisson/log
families. The offset $o_{it}$ is known, not estimated. Unit and time IDs index
factor rows. The model does not automatically add separate unit and time
intercepts: represent desired additive terms explicitly or choose an
appropriate model specification.

Trex minimizes the **mean observed-cell** negative log likelihood, plus

$$
\frac{\lambda}{2}\{\operatorname{mean}(A^2)+\operatorname{mean}(B^2)\}
+\frac{\lambda_\beta}{2}\operatorname{mean}(\beta^2).
$$

The Gaussian loss is half the squared error. The factorization makes
optimization nonconvex; factor rescalings and rotations also make individual
factor coordinates non-unique. Interpret the product $AB'$ or predicted
means, not an arbitrary fitted axis as an identified economic trait.

## Worked example: Gaussian panel with masked cells

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from trex import LatentFactorGLM

torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.manual_seed(403)
N, T = 35, 20
X = torch.randn(N, T, 2, dtype=torch.float64)
beta = torch.tensor([0.9, -0.6], dtype=torch.float64)
A = torch.randn(N, 2, dtype=torch.float64)*0.6
B = torch.randn(T, 2, dtype=torch.float64)*0.6
offset = 0.1*torch.randn(N, T, dtype=torch.float64)
mean = X @ beta + A @ B.T + offset
y = mean + 0.1*torch.randn_like(mean)
mask = torch.rand(N, T) < 0.8
fit = LatentFactorGLM(
    family="gaussian", rank=2, penalty=1e-3,
    optimizer_kwargs={"lr": 0.04, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    maxiter=1400, tol=1e-8, device="cpu",
).fit(X, y, mask=mask, offset=offset)
pred = fit.predict_mean(X, offset=offset).detach()
pd.DataFrame({"Truth": beta.numpy(), "Estimate": fit.params["coef"].numpy()},
             index=["x1", "x2"]).round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-factor-holdout
#| fig-cap: "Predictions for held-out cells. The diagonal represents exact prediction of the latent conditional mean."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(mean[~mask].numpy(), pred[~mask].numpy(), alpha=0.6, s=16)
ax.plot([-3, 3], [-3, 3], "k--")
ax.set(xlabel="True conditional mean", ylabel="Fitted mean")
plt.show()
print("Held-out RMSE against noisy outcomes:", float(((pred[~mask]-y[~mask])**2).mean().sqrt()))
```

## Binary and count outcomes

Changing the family changes the likelihood and inverse link, not merely a
post-processing transform of a least-squares fit. Here is a rank-zero Poisson
fit, a useful reference case for the nonlinear implementation.

```{python}
torch.manual_seed(404)
count_X = torch.ones(N, T, 2, dtype=torch.float64)
count_X[:, :, 1] = torch.randn(N, T, dtype=torch.float64)*0.5
exposure = 0.7 + torch.rand(N, T, dtype=torch.float64)
count_beta = torch.tensor([-0.2, 0.4], dtype=torch.float64)
count_y = torch.poisson(torch.exp(count_X @ count_beta) * exposure)
count_fit = LatentFactorGLM(
    family="poisson", rank=0, penalty=0,
    optimizer_kwargs={"lr": 0.04, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    maxiter=800, tol=1e-8, device="cpu",
).fit(count_X, count_y, offset=exposure.log())
print("Poisson coefficients:", count_fit.params["coef"].numpy().round(3))
print("Mean fitted count:", float(count_fit.predict_mean(count_X, offset=exposure.log()).mean()))
```

For Bernoulli responses choose `family="bernoulli"` and call
`predict_proba`. For either family, `predict_index` returns $\eta$, whereas
`predict_mean` applies the inverse link. Trex caps very large log rates in
Poisson prediction for numerical safety; inspect extreme-index fits rather
than treating saturation as evidence of a well-behaved model.

## Layout and limitations

Dense input uses `X.shape == (N,T,p)` and `y.shape == (N,T)`. An observation
list uses `(n_obs,p)` and explicit `unit_ids` and `time_ids`. A boolean mask
selects training observations in either layout; predictions still require
levels represented in the fitted model. This is not a cold-start embedding
model for new units or dates.

Use multiple starts and time- or block-aware validation for rank and penalty.
The current implementation does not report identification-aware coefficient
or treatment-effect covariance estimates. With short panels, nonlinear
incidental parameters can matter. Interactive effects are a model for
unobserved heterogeneity, not by themselves a causal identification strategy.
